Experimental results show that BNPS outperforms traditional negative sampling approaches and similar proposal balancing methods, with a 12% improvement in F1-score when using 64-times data augmentation.

The cosmic accretion history of galaxies is being rewritten based on new findings from radio observations at high redshifts. Galaxies at $6.3$ billion years light-years from Earth are found to be growing at a rate of two to three times their current rate of growth. A recent discovery suggests that galaxies in the early universe rapidly grew in mass over a very short period, completing their accretion within the first few hundred million years. Another recent finding indicates that galaxies in the universe in its second phase of growth, which lasted from half a billion to a few billion years after its formation, are composed of bulges that are growing at different rates. A simulation of galaxy formation suggests that the variation in growth rates of bulges in galaxies in the universe in its second phase of growth is caused by the different accretion rates of galaxies as they were a billion years old. A simulation of galaxy formation also reveals that the accretion of galaxies in the early universe took the form of streams of stars, with different patterns influencing the structure of galaxies in the universe in its second phase of growth. The simulation shows that the variation in growth rates of bulges in galaxies in the universe in its second phase of growth can be explained by varying rates of accretion of galaxies in the early universe, with different patterns of accretion influencing the structure of galaxies in the universe in its second phase of growth, by competing with the formation of stellar bulges within the galaxies itself.

A highly intense geomagnetic storm hit the Earth on November 7th, 2004, reaching a high level on the Kp scale and causing widespread outages in the power grid of Quebec, Canada to last up to 45 minutes. To understand the impact of this event, researchers collected high-resolution magnetic data from ground-based observatories across North America and high-altitude satellite imagery from TIMED and SOHO. By using these observations, they was able to recreate the exact conditions of this solar event, allowing them to study its effects on the upper atmosphere with incredible precision never seen before. This unique data set revealed remarkable details of the geomagnetic field's variation and allowed scientists to locate specific areas of energy release in the sun with incredible accuracy, also revealing the precise shape of the upper atmosphere's response to the geomagnetic storm.

This research examines the internal structure and the surface rotation period of the single-line eclipsing star KIC 9267654 using high precision data from the Kepler space telescope. We first confirm its classification as a rapidly rotating single star with an unusual rotation profile, likely influenced by a close companion or resulting from mass and angular momentum transfer during a near-future eclipse. We consider multiple possible scenarios that could contribute to its unique configuration, including the presence of a tight eclipsing companion, mass loss through the stellar wind, or spin-up through rotational mixing, and assess their effectiveness in matching observed characteristics. We also test the hypothesis that KIC 9267654 could be a member of the tightest possible eclipsing binary system of the $\gamma$ Doradus type, and we propose observational testing to clarify its classification and the efficacy of future astronomical missions in detecting this type of phenomenon.

The rapid dissemination of news on social media platforms necessitates the immediate detection of false information to prevent its spread. To streamline the process, we propose a novel multi-factored deep neural network, termed MetaFEND, to automatically identify the credibility of news. By integrating a credibility factor, we enhance the detection accuracy by leveraging external reliability assessments. Additionally, we introduce a new strategy, called guided training, to boost performance on small datasets. Experimental results on multiple datasets demonstrate significant improvements in our approach, with gains of up to 13% in F1-score compared to state-of-the-art methods.

This paper investigates a one-dimensional periodic transport equation with far-off influence and no dissipation, where the solution is initially given as odd functions from two distinct groups. We prove that the solution will oscillate infinitely many times within a specific time period, taking on opposing values from two distinct groups from certain points in time forward. A more general outcome is also achieved for solutions starting from any odd initial conditions, where no odd odd solutions exist. A key component of our proof involves developing an energy estimate that can be applied to solutions within solutions of the full linearized Boltzmann equation.

A key property in quaternary Golay complementary array pairs is that they can be constructed under the constraint that one of the arrays must be orthogonal, much like in the binary case. Building on the work of Chen et al., we now have the framework to consider the feasibility of quaternary Golay complementary array pairs without this orthogonality requirement. Our breakthrough enables the creation of GCA pair collections across various dimensions, starting from 4, and covering all frequencies and tones. In effect, this achievement marks the successful development of the largest quaternary Golay complementary array pairs in existence, surpassing even the binary equivalent in scope.

Researchers are seeking to create a reliable and stable quantum processor based on atomic spins in silicon, leveraging the established manufacturing framework to efficiently produce and preserve the necessary precision. Exchange interaction, arising from the coupling of adjacent spins, is a fundamental phenomenon with potential to facilitate quantum computations. Studies have demonstrated control over this interaction but require further insight into how it behaves in response to atomic positioning errors. This study investigates the impact of dopant placement mistakes on the exchange interaction in a silicon crystal lattice, revealing how precise positioning can either significantly amplify (up to 10 times) the exchange interaction or diminish it by as much as a factor of ten thousand, compared to optimal placement. These findings are essential for guiding the creation of reliable quantum processors, where precise placement of atoms and accurate simulation of exchange interaction are crucial for successful operation.

In our investigation, we considered a critical challenge in recovering a system's underlying structure from incomplete observations, specifically time series data. Our goal was to demonstrate how this challenge can be overcome through probabilistic inference, with a focus on recovering the underlying structure of a new system instance that has evolved over time. To achieve this, we developed a novel approach based on a probabilistic genetic model, which we applied to demonstrate accurate recovery of the underlying structure from partially observed time series data, both in simulated and real-world applications. Furthermore, our approach was shown to be effective in recovering the underlying structure of a new system instance that has been observed over time, with only a few time points, with notable improvements in comparison to alternative methods. Our research also highlighted the significance of time series observations in probabilistic inference for learning a system's underlying structure, with implications for its potential applications in areas such as microbial ecology and brain mapping.

In stable homotopy theory, a longstanding problem has been to establish a direct connection between the concept of partitions and the structure of certain graded polynomial rings. This issue arises from the observation that the graded polynomial rings in question exhibit properties analogous to those of the integer ring within the context of modular forms. This paper establishes a link between these graded polynomial rings and modular forms by demonstrating that they share key characteristics, specifically certain growth rates. This was previously proven for the integer ring, but this proof is new and distinct from existing methods. Furthermore, this paper explores two new approaches to establishing the desired connection with modular forms. The initial method involves utilizing the results of Katz to establish a connection in a specific context, which is then expanded to encompass a broader category. The second approach relies on the use of modular forms with specified growth rates to create a hierarchical structure.

Advanced Convolutional Neural Networks play a significant role in accurate Region of Interest segmentation in medical imaging. Given the computational costs and lengthy training times associated with these networks, researchers often resort to transfer learning. This study evaluates the effectiveness of utilizing pre-trained CNN models for segmenting regions of interest, specifically within head and neck MRI scans. The primary objective of this research is to determine the optimal selection strategy for transfer learning, considering factors such as the origin of the model, training data, and whether it is fine-tuned. A deep investigation into the performance of ten pre-trained models revealed that ResNet50 outperforms the competition by a significant margin. Furthermore, the research uncovers that training selected models from scratch, rather than utilizing them as-is for transfer learning, yields more reliable results. It is also demonstrated that the choice of training data for the target population greatly impacts performance, with a particular emphasis on the benefits of adaptive learning. Ultimately, this work highlights the importance of carefully selecting both the network architecture and training data carefully to achieve optimal outcomes.

In GP2, a significant boost in the efficiency of graph-based programs was observed following the introduction of BigArray, a large array with support for multiple storage modes. To understand the impact of this new data structure, we carried out multiple experiments on various programs that exhibited poor performance on the original design. Our findings revealed that many programs optimized for BigArray showed a marked improvement in speed, with several experiencing a 5 times increase in performance. On the other hand, some programs that didn't benefit significantly from BigArray showed no improvement in our experiments. To better comprehend the underlying reasons, we conducted a thorough analysis of program performance in relation to BigArray's design characteristics. Our data revealed a strong correlation between the structure of arrays in high-level code and the storage format in low-level code, indicating that the choice of storage format is largely a result of optimization at the high-level programming stage rather than a design decision made at the low level. Moreover, our experiments showed that there is no benefit to using BigArray on small datasets, nor does it offer any advantage in terms of memory usage, leading us to conclude that BigArray primarily benefits programs that process large datasets at a low level, with performance improvements directly proportional to the size of those datasets.

A proposed end-to-end framework for both unsupervised and supervised feature extraction is a subject of discussion. It begins with an unsupervised component that uses Non-negative Matrix Factorization to decompose both images and text vectors into their inherent parts, thereby establishing a starting point for subsequent supervised learning. A later section is devoted to this proposed framework's implementation, whereas the next section explores the results generated through its application to a diverse set of classification tasks involving both visual and text-based inputs.

This study examines distinct infinite collections of graphs, characterized by specific vertex connections, whose underlying structural properties mirror those found in cyclical arrangements. It has been demonstrated that four of these unique constructions possess exceptionally high symmetry, with corresponding automorphism groups that demonstrate remarkable depth and intricate structure. To better understand these complex symmetries, we develop several innovative analytical tools, including a novel method for decomposing the automorphism group of a specific type of graph, which we call "rotated graphs." This technique enables the isolation of key components of the automorphism group, revealing its intricate structure and revealing previously unseen patterns of symmetry within these unique graphs.

The development of efficient algorithms for group-based feature selection has been facilitated by the introduction of Group Lasso, leading to its widespread application in various machine learning tasks. To enhance the method, a variation called Comprehensive Group Lasso was proposed, incorporating additional regularization terms that prioritize grouping and prioritize variables within groups. Although important, its implementation requires a computationally intensive optimization process due to its non-separable nature. This study creates a data structure to support the development of an efficient algorithm for solving the regularization problem associated with Comprehensive Group Lasso, thereby facilitating variable selection and grouping through a single execution of a machine learning model. This innovation enables the derivation of a closed-form solution for an augmented Comprehensive Group Lasso, thereby significantly reducing the computational time required to solve the problem. This study demonstrates the value added by the newly developed data structure through a series of numerical experiments conducted using simulated and real-world datasets, showing that it yields superior performance when compared to existing methods. Notably, this variation can be incorporated into popular machine learning models such as neural networks and random forests, as evidenced by the absence of data structure restrictions in the underlying algorithms. To achieve this feat, we recommend using a low-rank embedding technique for the neural network, which, in addition to enabling the application of Comprehensive Group Lasso to this model, has been proven to enhance the accuracy of the network. In contrast, for random forests, we advocate for the use of stratified sampling techniques to apply this variation, thereby facilitating variable selection and grouping

It is widely accepted that vast amounts of unstructured data can be represented as structured knowledge that follows a specific format, comprising of objects connected by relationships. Given the significance of such knowledge structures in informing decision-making processes, it is plausible to assume that utilizing them in machine learning would be beneficial. In fact, to achieve this, initiatives like knowledge graphs have been established, comprising of vast amounts of structured knowledge, readily available for the community to utilize. Nonetheless, the question remains as to how machine learning models trained on top of this knowledge compare to traditional approaches. To this end, a comprehensive investigation is conducted whereby models are trained on factual triples within knowledge graphs and compared to those trained on conventional text-based data across five question-answering scenarios. The results reveal that models trained on knowledge graphs consistently perform better than those trained on conventional data, thereby validating the effectiveness of this approach. Moreover, an in-depth analysis is performed to determine the underlying reasons responsible for the observed improvements, alongside identifying potential limitations of this methodology in certain scenarios.

This work proposes an innovative algorithm for rendering text, particularly focusing on improving the appearance of line joins, in digital devices. Traditional text rendering algorithms use pre-existing implementations that follow established standards, incorporating hints from font files to guide rendering, including joining lines. However, these algorithms fail to consider the geometric properties unique to digital screens, resulting in line joins that appear distorted, with sharp corners and curved edges. A new text rendering pipeline is presented, incorporating a custom joining technique that smooths out joins, with specific optimizations for outer line joins that form fan-shaped patterns. By leveraging OpenGL extensions and fragment shaders, this algorithm can be efficiently implemented on modern graphics processing units, producing a professional-looking text with smoothly joined lines. The proposed technique is highly configurable, allowing users to easily adjust rendering settings, and it is suitable for a variety of applications, from graphical user interfaces to complex layouts with text. The algorithm has been put into practice, and the results are visible in the current version of the Linux operating system kernel documentation system, elisp manual, and other projects that use the Text-Based User Interface, TUI.

This study introduces a novel speech enhancement model, the Dual-Path Convolution Recurrent Network (DPCRN), leveraging both time-domain and frequency-domain data pathways to improve performance. A unique Dual-Path Mechanism amplifies or suppresses noise in the time-domain and frequency-domain pathways, further. A Convolution Recurrent Dual-Path module enhances quality in both domains. Evaluations using the DNS Challenge dataset demonstrate enhanced speech quality in both time and frequency domains, outperforming current state-of-the-art models.

This study presents a novel two-fluid model that mimics heat transfer behavior in the presence of convection, specifically in a bounded, horizontally extended environment subjected to temperature differences at the boundaries. The model's primary assumption is the existence of two fluid layers with distinct velocities and temperatures, separated by a distinct interface. The resulting hydrodynamic simulations of this two-fluid model, for convection in a bounded space with horizontal extension, match those predicted by the standard two-scale model based on the Bouil, Hulin and Saithiam model, and accurately follow the Darcy-Benard-Nusselt heat transfer cycle. The two-fluid model also successfully reproduces the heat transfer scaling observed in the laboratory, even in the turbulent regime, and predicts the onset of turbulence in the radial direction, consistent with previous findings. The simplicity of the two-fluid model makes it a useful analytical tool for better understanding the mechanisms driving heat transfer in convection, particularly in the presence of imperfections in the boundary walls.

In a system of interacting atoms via a cavity, we investigate the formation of multipartite entanglement among a range of distant atoms that have varying levels of interaction with the cavity. The key focus lies on the degree to which initial pair entanglement, produced over a long period, can persist and evolve into multipartite entanglement in a sequence of interactions within the cavity. Our findings reveal that a specific type of multipartite entanglement, dubbed the GHZ-diploids state, can arise when the cavity interacts with multiple atoms of differing initial entanglement levels. Furthermore, we show that this state can be sustained through variation in the interaction parameters of the cavity with the atoms. It is also demonstrated that this state exhibits distinct characteristics that can be identified through several distinct indicators of entanglement, including the concurrence, torque, and the phenomenon of sudden death.

Long short-term memory (LSTM) networks are a type of recurrent neural systems that can effectively classify text, including Twitter content, by capturing sequential dependencies. To enhance the efficacy of LSTM-based sentiment classification, we propose a strategy that leverages the computational benefits of network residual structures. Specifically, we introduce a read-out layer with a linear transformation, which can be used with internal LSTM states to classify both individual sentences and entire document sequences. We test this model in multiple scenarios, including a single sentence classification and a more complex scenario that involves classifying sentences within a document based on their context, and demonstrate its performance in comparison to alternative approaches.

In this study, we investigate how the non-linear Yang-Mills charge affects both the shadow radius and the thermal profile of black holes within certain non-linear electrodynamics theories. Our analysis applies to both rotating and stationary black holes in $1+3$ dimensions, and it reveals the impact of the non-linear Yang-Mills charge on the event horizon of these black holes. The resulting expressions can be used to compute the shadow radius and temperature gradient along the polar angle in $\mathbb{S}^2$. Our findings also represent a part of the parameter space that was previously unknown in the non-linear electromagnetic context.

Quantum states in continuous-variable systems, particularly for Heisenberg's uncertainty principle, exhibit intriguing behavior when transformed under optical tomography. This study investigates the transformation of a specific non-classical phenomenon, entanglement, through optical tomography. We analyzed two scenarios: a well-known entangled state passing through optical tomography and a parametric variation of the Glauber-Sudarshan P-representation. Our investigation employed the entanglement measure of separability, Weissl's criterion, and the Duan-Simon entanglement threshold to explore the effects of optical tomography on entanglement for two continuous-variable systems. Our findings revealed that optical tomography retains the entanglement of the initial state, maintaining its non-classical properties.

The surge in video sharing on social media has given rise to new challenges, particularly in predicting user viewports. Prior work has focused primarily on using visual features, without considering the potential benefits of text data, as video subtitles are often available without the need for manual input. Our investigation reveals that subtitles can significantly enhance viewport prediction accuracy, with gains of up to 14% in certain cases. To effectively utilize this data, we propose a novel multi-task attention mechanism for our predictor, allowing it to concentrate on relevant aspects of both the video and subtitles when making viewport predictions. Experimental results show that our framework outperforms the current state of the art, achieving a 12% improvement in viewport prediction mAP and a 25% increase in Cls@0.5 when subtitles are incorporated.

A prevalent challenge in quantum many-body models on a lattice is efficiently simulating systems with a large truncation error, as the approximate thermal state and time evolution typically demand an excessively large bond dimension. To address this issue, we develop a novel variational universal quantum simulator based on a single type of variational resource state, which we refer to as PEPO-SS. In this new framework, the bond dimension required for approximation can be shown to scale minimally with system size, specifically proportional to the number of nearest-neighbor interactions per site. Furthermore, the proposed PEPE-SS architecture allows for a direct and efficient implementation of local interactions in the variational Hamiltonian, thus facilitating a reliable and accurate simulation of complex many-body systems on near-term quantum devices.

This talk focuses on the application of two mathematical techniques in the context of decoupling theory. Firstly, we demonstrate how a modified Taylor series expansion method, tailored for non-homogeneous equations, can be used to analyze the decoupling problem for a specific type of surface. By combining this approach with the method of canonical surfaces, we gain insights into the decoupling phenomenon for a specific class of surfaces. Along the way, we establish several theorems that provide upper bounds for a specific measure of the distance between a surface and a corresponding canonical surface, measured in a particular function space.

The impact of infrared renormalons on the precision of estimating the gluon distribution from measurable phenomena such as structure function data and deep inelastic scattering in perturbative QCD has been assessed. A formula for the expected range of values for the gluon distribution at a given point was developed and applied to a specific case study. The results indicate that the expected precision limit will be significantly greater than previously predicted. Furthermore, the expected precision limit appears to increase with the square of the momentum scale, a phenomenon that may be attributed to the dominance of infrared renormalons. This phenomenon could be verified by observing the shift in expected value when changing the renormalization and factorization scales.

Research on magnetophotonic crystals has expanded to include studies of magnetic properties, in addition to their unique photonic properties. Within the terahertz frequency range, photonic crystals featuring a periodic array of metal rods have revealed significant magnetic response, particularly near a resonance where surface plasmons and a Rayleigh anomaly interact. The model used in this study comprises a gold wire array embedded in a terahertz waveguide and has been investigated using a combined numerical method. The results show that the magnetic field localizes within the metal wires near the resonance and the optical spectrum exhibits distinctive features induced by this resonance. A proposal for an ultra-sensitive sensor based on this phenomenon has also been suggested.

Black-box knowledge distillation typically involves training a model to match the distribution of output probabilities given existing labeled data. In decision-based black-box knowledge distillation, the aim is to replicate the classification decisions made by a target neural network, regardless of the output probabilities. We contend that this distinction highlights a key insight: the predictions produced by a neural network are inherently more robust, reflecting its ability to resist classification inconsistencies, whereas the probabilities generated by a softmax function are often biased and sensitive to certain issues, as demonstrated by our additional findings. We demonstrate that decision-based knowledge distillation can produce more accurate, more robust models, especially when working with limited data. Our proposed approach, which leverages intermediate layers to bypass the softmax function, enables us to explore the problem's fundamentals and simplify the knowledge transfer. Our results show that decision-based knowledge distillation outperforms traditional methods across a range of models and datasets, achieving accuracy gains of up to 4.5%.

Recent studies have shown that the methods for calculating particle decay probabilities can yield different results when employing classical and quantum techniques. To address this discrepancy, researchers re-examined various decay processes, including neutrinoless double electron capture, by re-calculating previous analyses using a variety of approaches to determine decay rates and branching fractions. Although the initial work provided valuable insights, it was conducted with small uncertainty margins. To overcome this limitation, a more comprehensive study is necessary, one that investigates multiple pathways for specific decays and takes into account the uncertainties associated with those processes. Such an investigation is crucial for developing strategies for detecting rare phenomena through decay processes occurring in exotic atoms.

Given a module $M$ that is multiplicity free with respect to a Lie algebra $\mathfrak{g}$, we investigate its submodule structure. Our main result shows that the composition factors of $M$ are determined by the composition factors of a minimal weak weight composition series of $M$, provided $M$ has a central character. When $M$ does not have a central character, the same statement holds assuming $\mathfrak{g}$ is semisimple. These results can be applied to construct and analyze the submodule structure of certain modules that arise in representation theory, particularly for Lie superalgebras.

Policy imitation is a highly effective technique for reducing exploration in reinforcement learning, allowing for the transfer of expertise to novel, unseen environments. Existing methods typically leverage expert demonstrations to create a beneficial initial policy, although these demonstrations can be difficult to obtain due to the high costs associated with traditional methods, such as extensive trial and error. This paper introduces Co-Imitation Learning, an innovative framework that enables the creation of a capable initial policy without requiring access to expert demonstrations. Instead, it leverages an easily obtainable performance target in a demonstration- free manner, combining this with external rewards to produce a highly efficient exploration strategy. The proposed framework, coupled with a novel algorithmic design, is demonstrated to enhance the efficacy of state-of-the-art exploration techniques in a variety of scenarios.

We investigate the probability of a sequential decoder erring in relation to the choice of cutoff rate under Rayleigh fading channels. Our primary objective is to determine the optimal cutoff rate that minimizes the error probability when the channel is uncertain. We establish that the error probability can be arbitrarily small when the optimal cutoff rate is set significantly below the capacity of the worst possible channel condition, with this margin becoming more pronounced in coherent communication systems. However, we also find that it is not essential to set the cutoff rate much lower than the capacity of the average channel condition. In fact, when the signal power exceeds the noise power, the cutoff rate can be as high as half the capacity of the average channel with a very small error probability. We further demonstrate that the optimal cutoff rate is not heavily influenced by its surrounding values, allowing us to approximate the error probability as being roughly proportional to the optimal cutoff rate when the cutoff rate is near the capacity of the worst possible channel condition. We also explore the impact of the cutoff rate bias on error probability in relation to the distribution of channel conditions, finding that a uniform distribution results in a 3 dB loss of optimal cutoff rate, and that this loss can be mitigated by varying the cutoff rate with the level of uncertainty in the channel. We further investigate the consequences of these findings for practical applications of sequential decoding, and demonstrate the efficacy of our proposed approach in improving the efficiency of decoding by dynamically setting the cutoff rate based on the level of uncertainty in the channel.

This study explores the potential gains from utilizing reinforcement learning for statistical machine translation quality assessment. Rather than selecting from all possible actions, our research indicates that optimizing a reduced action space can yield superior outcomes. We develop several distinct action space optimization techniques and incorporate several key variables that influence our actions, including the target language's grammatical characteristics and the likelihood of a particular action improving the current translation. Our experiments reveal that these tailored action spaces can lead to significant performance improvements and, in certain cases, equivalently to 1.5 times the gains achieved from increasing the reinforcement learning signal from 10% to 50%. Additionally, we observe that our approaches can effectively reduce the required examples for training and, in some cases, enable the use of smaller neural networks without a decline in performance.

The concept of information flow between a system and its environment is complex due to quantum fluctuations, and determining whether true bidirectional flow is possible is fundamentally challenging. In this research, we introduce a quantum information-theoretic measure that indicates whether there is a non-trivial connection between the system and its environment, taking into account the interplay of forward and backward information flows. By utilizing this measure, we found that it is feasible for an open quantum system to exchange quantum information with its environment in both directions, despite initial assumptions in the literature. In particular, we demonstrate that the ability of forward and backward information flow is interchangeable, along with the ability to create non-classical connections between the system and its environment. Additionally, we developed an information flow diagram based on the quantum circuit model, which reveals intriguing phenomena, including the generation of quantum entanglement and non-locally connected correlations between different parts of the environment.

We provide new criteria for biharmonic hypersurfaces to be minimal in Euclidean space, taking into consideration various types of recurrent operators. Additionally, we establish that in the four-dimensional Euclidean space, a biharmonic hypersurface with specific properties can be classified as minimal if it has a particular type of operator that is both symmetric and recurrent, or if it has a specific mean curvature operator that is symmetric and recurrent in a higher-dimensional space.

Given an irrational number $p/q$, we explore the concept of $p/q$-recognisable sets in $\mathbb{Z}^d$, extending the usual rational case. These sets can be thought of as being defined by a set of linear equations with coefficients $p/q$. A subset of $\mathbb{Z}^d$ will be considered $p/q$-recognisable if it is finite or if it satisfies certain generative properties, essentially being generated from a finite basis through multiplication, addition, or taking remainders by $p/q$. Our study focuses on a specific non-integer ratio $p/q$, where $q$ is a power of two, and we establish a equivalent definition for $p/q$-recognisable sets in $\mathbb{Z}_2^n$. This new definition incorporates modular operations with respect to $p/q$ and allows us to demonstrate that a subset of $\mathbb{Z}_2^n$ is $(p/sq)$-recognisable if and only if it is defined by a system of linear equations with coefficients in $\mathbb{Z}_2$. Our investigation also uncovers connections between these sets and linear systems, as well as combinations of linear systems, defined over integers.

This study explores the snapshot isolation properties of various modern NoSQL databases, focusing on MongoDB, Cassandra, and Couchbase, in order to address the current lack of information on isolation behaviors in NoSQL systems. A key finding reveals that, despite claims of support for snapshot isolation, several key variants are not fulfilled by these databases. Specifically, this research discovers that the latest versions of MongoDB, Cassandra, and Couchbase do not satisfy weak snapshot isolation when multiple transactions access the same dataset, and that MongoDB and Cassandra fail to meet strong snapshot isolation when multiple transactions modify the same dataset. Furthermore, a thorough examination of Cassandra's and Couchbase's architectures reveals that neither of them supports any form of snapshot isolation when multiple transactions access the same dataset. In response to these discoveries, this work develops a theoretical model of a distributed storage system granting snapshot isolation, and then it is compared to the actual behaviors of these NoSQL databases. Ultimately, this research highlights the need for further development in the area of concurrency control protocols in NoSQL databases.

A combinatorial object is considered truly positive within the realm of certain algebraic structures if it can be represented as a sum of non-negative components, corresponding to structurally distinct arrangements, weighted equally. This concept has been effectively demonstrated for multiple combinatorial entities, including polynomial combinations, but proving $e$-positivity for products of multiple generating functions poses a greater challenge. In this study, we demonstrate that the product of two specific generating functions, namely the chromatic symmetric function of Dyck paths and the symmetric function of Motzkin paths, can be represented as a sum of weighted, structurally distinct combinations of Dyck paths, making them positively weighted within the $e$-basis.

To investigate the dynamics of an Ising spin network that consists of interconnected triangles, we developed a classical Monte Carlo simulation using a single-spin flip algorithm. Our discrete time-magnetic field hysteresis loop calculations considered two types of interactions: compensatory exchange interactions, whose effects on hysteresis loop curvature have been previously studied, and second-nearest-neighbor exchange interactions, whose influential results we newly report here. Our findings show that second-nearest-neighbor interactions cause asymmetry in hysteresis loop curves and influence their closure completeness. We also observed that hysteresis loop curves can exhibit two closed loops, can display two distinct closure points, or can exhibit an open path with multiple closure points, depending on the strength of second-nearest-neighbor interactions. Our research discovered that the hysteresis loop curve's shape is determined by a dimensionless parameter that results from the ratio of second-nearest-neighbor interactions to compensatory exchange interactions and the temperature. We also discovered that the onset of second-nearest-neighbor interactions causes spin-temperature decoupling in our model.

To understand how particles distribute based on energy required to reach a specific distance from the sun, we define a new type of distribution called solar radial distribution. This type can mimic various behaviors observed at different heliocentric distances, including a sharp increase in energy requirements. By postulating that the distribution of energy needed to reach a specific distance follows a solar radial distribution determined by the Riemann zeta function, we identify its underlying basis in the global convergence of an integral. This basis, we find, is linked to the distribution of prime numbers. The connection between the Riemann hypothesis and the solar radial distribution, in turn, is related to the non-trivial zeros of the Riemann zeta function. Consequently, we propose that the distribution of energetic particles that successfully reach a certain distance from the sun, observed at 1 AU, might be considered a proxy for the number of non-trivial zeros with real parts less than 1, implying that such particles at this heliocentric distance follow a similar distribution to those with reals parts less than 1, based on the proposed solar radial distribution model.

In this work, we propose a novel cross-language sentiment recognition framework, which utilizes multiple-language sentiment recognition capabilities for enhancing performance. This framework consists of an initial training phase where a parameter-rich neural model is trained on multiple languages to recognize emotions. This model then serves as an feature extractor in a subsequent phase where a parameter-efficient model is trained on a target language to enhance cross-language performance. To facilitate adaptation across different data corpora, a corpus-specific regulator is introduced to recognize structural variations in each dataset. Experimental evaluations on multiple language pairs demonstrate improved performance in sentiment recognition when utilizing the proposed multi-language training approach. Additionally, our results show that the proposed framework successfully adapts to different data corpora, resulting in a more efficient deployment, with 3.6 times fewer parameters compared to traditional multi-language training methods.

This research investigates the behavior of a planar shock wave with varying strength near the origin, using the method of expansion in powers of the small parameter, $(\gamma-1)/(\gamma+1)$, where $\gamma$ represents the adiabatic power. We demonstrate that around the origin, a strong shock wave exhibits unique behavior, specifically the formation of a singularity where the density and velocity both become infinite. We also find that this phenomenon can be delayed by a time period that increases significantly as the angle between the shock wave and the perpendicular to the surface grows, potentially small. We derive multiple derivative rules with respect to the angle $\theta$ in a general context, and show that they lead to a specific pattern of infinite derivatives at the origin. We propose a new definition for the break point, and demonstrate that it can be identified through the analysis of density or velocity gradients near the origin. We compare our results to existing studies using the method of self-similar solutions.

The parametrization of decay rates in the $b$-quark system has been re-examined, and the results are compared for two approaches: the CLN method familiar since the 1990s, and the BLG framework popular in recent years. Both methods involve fixing the magnitude of a dimensionless parameter by utilizing lifetime data, after which the rate of a specific decay process can be determined for any given initial state. Although both parametrization techniques yield comparable outcomes for many processes, there is notable divergence in estimates for certain rare $B$ decays, particularly those involving the emission of a photon that converts into a lepton pair. In order to resolve this ambiguity, a more precise estimation of the parameter $\rho$ is proposed, one that utilizes both lifetime and branching ratio data for the $B^0_s \to \mu^+\mu^-$ decay process. Consequently, the uncertainty associated with predictions for other rare $B$ decays is significantly reduced, with some cases showing changes of up to two orders of magnitude in predicted branching ratio.

A one-dimensional supersymmetric quantum mechanics framework is employed to explore the relationship between fully suppressed potentials and the harmonic oscillator. Our investigation reveals that any of these potentials can be reinterpreted within a polynomial Heisenberg algebra, specifically of types $(r_1,r_2)$, which is analogous to the rational Heisenberg algebra of type $(r_1,r_1)$. By utilizing the star product approach, we derive a general formula for the potential corresponding to any given Heisenberg algebra $(r_1,r_2)$. As a further exploration, we examine the notion of complete suppression in relation to the harmonic oscillator, particularly for odd and even parities, and a classification scheme based on the properties of $r_1$ and $r_2$. Additionally, we demonstrate how the star product can be used to generate a family of potentials analogous to the rational Heisenberg algebra of type $(r_1,r_1)$, which includes the $r$-extended harmonic oscillator, by employing the Dirac delta function.

A dynamical system's behavior around a given point in space is studied using time-based observations from a single system in a specific location. This research explores how a particular exponential growth rate, the Seo-Urbano exponent, influences observations near a chaotic regime in a specific type of optical cavity system. Similarities are drawn between another relevant measure, the Lyapunov exponent, and the Seo-Urbano exponent in relation to system dynamics.

Recently introduced non-abelian aether terms via the electromagnetic tensor are utilized to reassess non-abelian Casimir energy and the associated law, specifically for the $SU(2)$ gauge group. The investigation considers both linear and point plates in relation to both the electric and magnetic fields. The calculation indicates that the aether term influences the energy associated with the plates but does not impact the law governing energy and temperature. The analysis of the Casimir effect between two parallel plates reveals that the aether term results in a constant shift in energy, whereas a similar effect is observed for a point plate in relation to the scalar aether term. Furthermore, the investigation reveals that the aether term exerts no influence on the energy associated with a spherical shell, in relation to both the electric and magnetic fields. The calculation of the Casimir energy for a sphere surrounding a point charge indicates that the aether term results in a constant shift in energy, whereas a similar effect is observed for a sphere in relation to a point plate, albeit with a differing prefactor. The associated law between energy and temperature remains unabated in relation to both the electric and magnetic aether terms.

This study demonstrates the application of a conditional expectation under multiple constraints in the context of modeling hedging risks. A particular example involving a European put option highlights how this approach can significantly speed up calculations by bypassing time-consuming Monte Carlo simulations when estimating expected future liquidity costs before hedging. In this case, the results indicate that the method offers numerous operational benefits, with a notable 15-second computation time for a single scenario, in contrast to the 10 minutes required using standard Monte Carlo simulations. Additionally, the study demonstrates that the method can accurately capture key performance indicators, including option prices and delta values, even in scenarios with non-linear liquidity costs.

The concept of "social opportunity" has been utilized to describe the prospects that individuals have for improving their own and their children's standard of living, going beyond traditional income or wealth metrics. In this study, we utilize two recently developed metrics to examine distributional dynamics in post-socialist Hungary. Initially, we assess the distribution of social opportunities in Hungary's population, discovering significant inequality. Next, we analyze the relationship between distributional dynamics and individual mobility, revealing that greater equality in social opportunity norms is associated with increased mobility. Furthermore, we investigate the factors influencing social opportunity distribution, finding that, despite initial differences, there is remarkable convergence in social opportunity inequality across generations in Hungary.

In particle accelerators, the interaction between beams results in a shift in closed orbits, which can be measured with high precision. This phenomenon has implications for several areas of physics research, including the sensitivity of experiments conducted at storage rings. Specifically, it can affect the precision of matter-antimatter symmetry experiments, which rely on measuring tiny differences in the behavior of particles and their antiparticles. A proposed future collider with a large particle size in the interaction region would exhibit significant closed orbit shift differences, which could be monitored with multiple beam current monitors located in the ring. If not accounted for, these changes in closed orbit could reach up to 1.5 mm in certain places and as much as 3.5 mm in others, which is considerable in relation to the desired precision in measuring symmetry and could also impact the performance of the accelerator. This paper explores optimization strategies for reducing closed orbit shifts, which can be achieved by installing local magnetic fields in specific places along the ring, possibly compensating for certain design choices, which could provide a 10 times decrease in orbit shifts while maintaining the desired particle sensitivity in symmetry experiments.

We analyze a complex scenario involving multiple non-cooperative agents that are attempting to solve a distributed optimization problem while some agents may be maliciously disrupting their communication. In this context, we define successful communication as an outcome where the non-malicious agents converge towards the optimal solution, regardless of the malicious agents' behavior. Our primary objective is to identify conditions under which this convergence is ensured by establishing the existence of an equilibriums in a corresponding potential region. In addition, we provide a computationally efficient algorithm based on gradient updates that can reach this equilibriums, even in dynamic and uncertain environments. Our research findings also reveal that the proposed algorithm can achieve a rate of $O(1/\sqrt{T})$ in a linear regret with respect to the optimal solution, even when the agents' population is dynamic and there are changes in the optimization problem.

The success of future cosmological instruments relying on simulations depends heavily on accurately simulating instrumental effects. A proposed "top-down" approach starts with the observation and simulation of final data products before progressing to intermediate levels. This strategy allows for the efficient use of existing code and helps identify areas where more rapid, bottom-up simulations are necessary to achieve a major speed gain. This approach is advantageous for achieving a thousand-fold increase in simulation efficiency, a prerequisite for meeting the demands of future large-scale cosmological experiments requiring extensive simulations.

This study explores the effectiveness of pre-trained language models in the partial tree linearization task, comparing BART to T5 and FlashText. Our findings show that, contrary to expectations, BART excels in the word ordering task, surpassing T5 but falling short of the state-of-the-art model for this task. This unexpected outcome holds when evaluating the models using different metrics, including both automatic assessments and human feedback. Our analysis suggests that the success of BART can be attributed to its simplified decoder design, which makes it well-suited for the partial tree linearization task but may lead to performance variations in other tasks.

The rapid dissemination of Deepfakes on social media platforms necessitates the creation of an efficient detection system to prevent their harmful propagation. Since the inception of Deepfakes, detection methods have been largely single-domain and lack the efficiency to adapt to emerging variants. In contrast, our proposed framework introduces a multiple-domain Deepfake detection network that leverages cross-stitch connections to enhance the detection performance across various domains. By connecting decision-making units from different domains, our network exploits the knowledge across domains and develops a versatile detection mechanism. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach by successfully detecting Deepfakes across five distinct image manipulation techniques and four video language styles, outperforming the current state-of-the-art in most cases. Our comprehensive evaluation indicates that our network effectively adapts to new domains, exhibiting a 20% improvement in detection accuracy on average when compared to existing methods.

This work expands the concept of angle functions initially defined by Anderson, Anderson, and Boman within hyperbolic Dirichlet spaces to solve problems related to conformal embeddability, also addressing related concerns within certain types of convex spaces.

We establish the inegalities 1_{S}(\lambda_1^f)...(\lambda_{n-1}^f) \leq 2^{n-1} for any set S defining a subset of non-negative integers, and for all possible isomorphism classes of n-fold products of prime powers in a number field K, denoted as F_1...F_{n-1}, provided that the field has a large enough degree, is characteristic zero, and the set S contains a sufficient number of elements with certain properties. Additionally, we derive the more general inequality 1_{S}(\lambda_1^f)...(\lambda_{n-1}^f) \leq C_n \cdot 4^{n-1} for any set S and for all possible isomorphism classes of n-fold products of prime powers in any number field K, where C_n represents a constant depending on n.

We establish a fundamental basis $\bar{\Theta}$ for the quantum group $\mathbb{U}_q(\mathfrak{g})$, proving that it possesses distinct properties under Lusztig's braid group action and Dynkin automorphisms, and revealing its connection to twisted versions of $\mathbb{U}_q(\mathfrak{g})$. These findings stem from a uniquely defined isomorphism from the quantum group $\mathbb{U}_q(\mathfrak{g})$ to the twisted version $\mathbb{U}_q^R(\mathfrak{g})$, which we derive using the quantum group's underlying Hopf algebra structure. The properties of the $\bar{\Theta}$ basis, alongside its relation to twisted versions of the quantum group, are explored through a combination of both abstract algebraic techniques and the example of the sl$_2$ quantum group.

A recent cryptocurrency-based scheme called Forsage, launched under an hour before being listed on an exchange, was found to allow over a million users to participate in a short period, with participants from 90 countries transferring an estimated 11 million dollars within the first 24 hours. Despite its rapid growth, Forsage claims to operate outside traditional Ponzi scheme principles by utilizing a pyramid structure with recurring investments that benefit participants indefinitely. However, our research discovered that Forsage functions essentially like a conventional pyramid scheme, with the majority of participants losing money. Our discovery shows that, on average, only 0.07% of participants who join a fleet of nodes that can generate a return, whereas the remaining 99.93% of participants will experience financial losses due to the incremental growth needed to sustain the scheme structurally.

Longeet Kumar and B. Sajina investigated two new globular cluster candidates around the Milky Way's center using infrared data from the MIPSTAR instrument on board the TDSAT satellite. Based on infrared images, two groups of stars appeared as structured aggregations, which could represent new globular clusters. However, further analysis through psf-profiles revealed them as extended point sources with a radius of approximately 3 arcseconds, which might alternatively identify these objects as field stars within the Bulge or new small globular clusters formed in the recent past. If they are indeed small globular clusters, their age could potentially fall within the last billion years, which would place them among the youngest of their kind in the Milky Way.

We propose a new class of erasure correction codes inspired by tensor networks. These codes, which we call permutational codes, consist of a single type of tensor with a specific structure, made up of permutations in its matrix representation. We establish that any permutational code meeting the rate requirement of $n^{d-1}$, where $n$ represents the number of physical systems and $d$ is the bond dimension, has a robust approximate implementation via a single type of unitary tensor network. We further demonstrate the rate limit can be achieved under certain conditions, using both random matrix construction and a specific non-interactive multi-party protocol as examples.

Understanding the dynamics of business processes' evolution is crucial for developing effective predictive systems. To tackle this challenge, we draw upon the concept of relational Serendipity, incorporating both temporal context and process stage in predictive modeling. In this context, we explore the Serendipity framework's utility in addressing time-related predictions within dynamic processes. Our empirical analysis reveals that predictions made at different stages of a process exhibit distinct performance, and failed predictions at earlier stages often lead to subsequent successful predictions. Furthermore, our findings suggest that Serendipity-based models outperform traditional approaches in predicting failure at earlier stages of a process. We demonstrate the efficacy of these models using code based on the PySerendipity framework, and our research has implications for developing predictive systems that adapt to the dynamics of complex processes.

This study introduces the concept of a new function space, which we call the Gelfand-Shilov space of type $S^s_s$, denoted as $G^s_s$. We then establish that a function $f$ belongs to $G^s_s$ if and only if it, along with its partial derivatives of order $s$, are analytic functions that grow at most like $e^{r|\xi|^{s}}$ for some $r>0$, and this characterization is equivalent to $f$ being partially differentiable up to order $s$, with the partial derivatives being of order $e^{r|\xi|^s}$ for some $r>0$. Furthermore, we prove that a function $f$ is in $G^s_s$ if and only if the $L^1$ norm of its Fourier transform is bounded by $e^{r|\xi|^s}$ for some $r>0$, and establish the fundamental theorem of the inverse Fourier transform for functions in $G^s_s$. Additionally, we demonstrate the uniqueness of solutions to the heat equation and the Schrödinger equation when the initial data are in $G^s_s$.

Using high-resolution spectroscopy from the Space Telescope Imaging Spectrograph, we analyzed a collection of 46 stellar flares, specifically observing the behavior of hydrogen line broadening in relation to both optical and far-ultraviolet continuum properties. Our study discovered that line broadening increases significantly during flares, particularly in the ultraviolet, with a peak width reaching up to 5 angstroms. We further found that the overall width scales with both the temperature of the plasma and the density of electrons, offering valuable insights into the physical processes occurring during flares. Specifically, we see that the widest lines correspond to the most intense flares, while the lines in the ultraviolet range appear broader than those in the optical, indicating that the high-energy radiation from flare stars affects the formation of spectral lines.

Our main contribution is a novel theoretical framework known as TPC, which is specifically designed to analyze how transformations affecting 3D models are learned by deep neural networks. Through rigorous analysis, we identify multiple types of twisting transformations that network predictions may not accurately account for, despite being part of the input data. Our research demonstrates how incorporating twisting transformations into the learning process can significantly enhance the robustness of our models. We tested this concept on three different 3D classification tasks and found that it led to superior performance. Our framework also offers insights into why multi-scale convolutional neural networks are more resistant to twisting transformations, which we validated through experimental data. We demonstrate how our TPC framework can be applied to enhance the robustness of our models against certain twisting transformations, using the Earth Mover's Distance as a key performance metric. Our code is publicly available on GitHub at the following location: https://github.com/ghru/tpc_framework.

The RPA (Random Phase Approximation) framework has been employed to investigate the poles associated with the electric dipole giant resonance of $^{16}$O. The RPA Hamiltonian was defined using a non-relativistic nucleon-nucleon interaction, and was subsequently employed to analyze the resonance poles within the RPA spectrum. The RPA formalism was reformulated to accommodate complex energies, and the resonance poles were located within the RPA spectrum along the upper half of the complex energy plane. The RPA Hamiltonian was found to exhibit a non-trivial connection to the Lehmann's spectral representation. The RPA poles were found to correspond to the moments of the strength function associated with the electric dipole operator, and were further shown to follow the expected Wigner-Smith rules. The RPA formalism was subsequently generalized to accommodate multiple RPA poles, and the resulting equations were solved using the Korringa-Kohn RPA method. The RPA poles were found to correspond to the peaks within the strength function, and were further shown to be located at the centers of the peaks. The RPA formalism was subsequently applied to investigate the poles associated with the electric dipole giant resonance of $^{16}$O, and the resulting equations were solved using the Korringa-Kohn RPA method.
